title: school
short_summary: The English word “school” comes through Old English and Latin from Ancient Greek skholḗ, a word originally associated with leisure or free time that later developed into the idea of learned discussion and formal instruction.
confidence_summary: The broad Greek → Latin → Old English → English route is well established. The semantic development from leisure to learned discussion and education is simplified here for prototype purposes.

lexical_info.main_definition: An institution, place, or system for education and instruction.
lexical_info.usage_note: Countable when referring to an institution, as in 'three schools'; often uncountable in phrases like 'go to school' or 'at school'.

forms.meaning: institution for education; group of students or teachers; system of instruction
school; lecture; learned discussion; group of pupils
leisure, free time; later discussion, lecture, place of learning

edges.note: Modern English school continues Old English scōl.
Old English scōl was borrowed from Latin schola.
Latin schola derives from Ancient Greek σχολή.

semantic_stages.label: Leisure / free time
semantic_stages.meaning: Ancient Greek skholḗ originally referred to leisure or free time.

semantic_stages.label: Discussion / lecture
semantic_stages.meaning: The word developed an association with learned discussion, lectures, or philosophical conversation conducted during leisure.

semantic_stages.label: Place of instruction
semantic_stages.meaning: The meaning shifted toward a place or institution where instruction takes place.

related_words.relationship: derived from the same Latin/Greek root
related borrowing/descendant ultimately from Latin schola

historical_context: The word’s development reflects a semantic path from leisure to learned discussion and finally to an institution dedicated to instruction. This makes it a useful example for semantic drift, not only geographic word migration.
